newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Investors cheer Gazprom promise but doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: Investors cheer Gazprom promise but doubts remain.

text.p: Pledges by Russian gas monopoly Gazprom to defend its segregated domestic and international share structure heartened foreign investors on Thursday but they said Gazprom was in no shape yet to tap foreigners for new funds.

Gazprom chairman Rem Vyakhirev said the firm was punishing foreign "swindlers" who bought cheaper shares on the domestic market, avoiding the three-fold premium on Gazprom American Depositary Shares (ADSs) which trade abroad.
Gazprom ADS prices leapt by 10 percent on the news.
Gazprom has repeatedly defended its two-tier share structure, and has set aside nine percent of its capital for non-resident investors.
ADSs are the only approved way foreigners can buy Gazprom equity, and Gazprom recently reinforced this by stopping an investment fund from buying domestic shares.
But analysts said Gazprom was in no shape to raise much-needed funds by issuing more of the expensive foreign shares as uncertainty about its ability to keep the two separate remained.

"There is enough unease about their ability at the present time to keep the two separate to make another one percent (ADS) placement at this time next to impossible," said one senior trader in Moscow.

The price of ADSs, which cover 10 underlying shares, rose to $17.50 at 1445 GMT in London from $15.90 at the previous close. The ADSs were launched at $15.75 in October and were trading over $23 in January.
Gazprom shares in Moscow ticked up to $0.6439 from $0.6415 on Thursday.
Gazprom has enormous natural resources but needs funds to build pipelines and pay off debt.

Russia accounts for a third of the world's gas reserves and 27 percent of its output. Gazprom accounts for about 95 percent of Russian output and is a key supplier to the western European natural gas market.
The company's debts to the state are huge, pegged last month at 14.8 trillion roubles ($2.6 billion), and it is building a multi-billion dollar pipeline to supply Europe.
But talk of another ADS issue, originally expected this year, have faded and Gazprom has focused on raising billions of dollars through syndicated loan credits.
Share analysts said the market was waiting for Gazprom's international accounts, due this summer, as well as an international audit of around 60 percent of its gas reserves, due this year.

"People have felt comfortable with Gazprom at this level," a Moscow trader said of the local shares. "We are not seeing any large wave of buying," he added, saying eyes were on the forthcoming international accounts.
Traders and analysts have welcomed new moves by Gazprom to improve transparency and open its doors to foreigners.

About 60 analysts and fund managers holding ADSs were shown around Gazprom's Siberian fields and briefed by top management on a five-day trip in April, said Byron Ousey, a director at Gazprom investor relations advisor Gavin Anderson.
"It was not a rearguard move," Ousey said from London. "Obviously Gazprom is facing up to the fact that it has a collection of major foreign shareholders whom it must respect."
"Anybody who comes to Moscow and wants to visit Gazprom will get an invitation to visit, provided they are bonefide professional fund managers," he said.
But the senior trader did not see it as preparation for attracting new investors soon. "They are being smart, looking at the long term."
Vyakhirev said: "By 1998 this company should start to take on a more normal form, in line with international standards,"
